summaries.headline: Rhode Island School Ties PBIS to Attendance Gains
summaries.summary: A Rhode Island assistant principal credits a positive behavioral interventions and supports framework with driving a significant boost in student attendance, using incentives tied to the same tiered structure schools already use for behavior management. Rather than treating attendance as a separate compliance issue, the school folded it into existing PBIS routines, recognizing students for consistent attendance the way they would for positive behavior. The approach suggests districts wrestling with chronic absenteeism may not need a new initiative from scratch but can extend systems already embedded in daily school culture.

summaries.headline: Math Educators Push Beyond Tricks, Shortcuts
summaries.summary: A new Education Week opinion roundup gathers veteran math educators reflecting on how instruction has shifted over the past decade and where it needs to go next. Contributor Alison Mello, a 30-year classroom veteran, argues the field's next chapter must move away from memorized tricks and shortcuts toward instruction built on genuine conceptual understanding. For district leaders shaping math curriculum and PD investments, the piece signals that practitioners themselves are calling for deeper instructional shifts, not just new materials or pacing guides.

summaries.headline: Anthropic Enters Crowded K-12 AI Classroom Race
summaries.summary: Anthropic has launched Claude for Teachers, a free AI assistant for verified K-12 educators that incorporates academic standards from all 50 states to help build lesson plans, personalize instructional materials, and analyze student data. The product enters a market already crowded with Google, OpenAI, and Khan Academy, all competing to embed their AI tools in classrooms nationwide, and Anthropic will pilot the tool in Detroit Public Schools as part of a study on educator well-being and practice. As AI companies race to shape how teachers work, districts are being asked to sort through competing products with limited independent evidence on which, if any, actually improve instruction or ease educator workload.

summaries.headline: Nebraska Head Starts Track Teacher Talk to Boost Literacy
summaries.summary: Seven rural and urban Head Start locations across Nebraska outfitted toddlers with recording devices this spring as part of a statewide push to increase the quantity and quality of adult-child conversations in early classrooms. The five-week program, run through a partnership between the Buffett Early Childhood Institute and the nonprofit Lena, reached more than 1,300 children and gave teachers data-driven feedback on their talk patterns, a method previously linked to higher reading scores. As states hunt for scalable ways to close early literacy gaps before kindergarten, this rollout offers a test case for whether coaching adults to talk more — and better — with young children can move the needle at a system level, not just in isolated classrooms.

summaries.headline: Memphis Charter Slashes Chronic Absenteeism to Near Zero
summaries.summary: Compass Berclair, a Memphis K-8 charter school, saw more than half its students chronically absent in 2022, but that number dropped to just three out of 230 students last year. Principal Kamie Cowan credits the turnaround to a dedicated attendance team that met biweekly starting in the 2022-23 school year to review data and set small, achievable goals rather than launching a sprawling initiative. The results land amid heightened scrutiny of Memphis-Shelby County Schools' districtwide attendance rates, which state lawmakers cited as one of six factors justifying an appointed oversight board now tied up in federal litigation.

summaries.headline: Science of Reading Push Skips High School, Leaders Say
summaries.summary: More than 40 states now mandate evidence-based reading instruction, but nearly all of that policy attention has concentrated on early grades, leaving district leaders without clear guidance for grades 9-12. School and district leaders working with literacy nonprofits have repeatedly asked for help identifying high-quality high school English materials, particularly ones that build knowledge through rigorous, content-rich texts and support older students who still struggle with grade-level reading. As elementary literacy reforms show measurable gains, the absence of a parallel framework for secondary schools leaves a critical gap for students who need strong reading instruction well beyond third grade.

summaries.headline: Chicago Schools Seek Vendors for SEL, Behavioral Health
summaries.summary: Chicago Public Schools, serving 316,000 students, is soliciting qualified vendors to provide social and emotional learning and behavioral health services on an as-needed basis, with proposals due Aug. 7. The district's request spans group and individual counseling, restorative practices, mentoring, parenting skills development, curriculum, and professional learning, and vendors must show evidence their approaches actually work. The scope of the solicitation signals how far SEL and behavioral health procurement has moved beyond isolated curriculum purchases into district-wide infrastructure for student support.

summaries.headline: States Escalate Legal Response to Chronic Absenteeism
summaries.summary: At least six states enacted laws this year targeting chronic absenteeism, defined as missing 10% or more of school days, roughly 18 days annually. Utah's new law creates an attendance monitoring system that flags at-risk students and can bring a class B misdemeanor charge against parents of grade 1-6 students after five truancies if they skip a required meeting with school officials, while Oregon now mandates public reporting of district-level attendance data and Vermont has overhauled its definitions and handling of absenteeism. The shift toward data transparency paired with parental accountability signals states are treating absenteeism less as a family issue and more as a system failure requiring measurable, enforceable intervention.

summaries.headline: CPS Closes Budget Gap With Layoffs, Furloughs Looming
summaries.summary: Chicago Public Schools unveiled a $9.88 billion budget that closes $450 million of its $732.5 million deficit through layoffs, new revenue, and other cuts, while holding five furlough days and a January spending freeze in reserve if state and city officials don't send more money. The district is cutting about 760 teaching positions and 800 school-based support staff this week, though most are expected to be rehired into vacancies elsewhere, and it's also betting on $200 million in city TIF surplus dollars — double what it projected last year. The budget adds roughly 900 special education teachers and aides even as general education staffing shrinks, a tradeoff that signals where CPS is willing to protect spending and where it isn't as it leans on Springfield and City Hall to avoid deeper mid-year cuts.

summaries.headline: Chicago Board Strikes Five School Board Candidates From Ballot
summaries.summary: Chicago's Board of Election Commissioners removed five school board candidates from November's ballot Tuesday, ruling against their petitions amid a broader signature-challenge process that has already touched 28 of the 51 original candidates. The decision leaves districts 8b and 9a with only one candidate each, joining districts 4b and 8a as uncontested races, while a pending ruling on a potential write-in campaign in district 10a could add a fifth. With 16 candidates' fates still undecided this month, the shrinking field of contested races raises real questions about how much genuine choice voters will have in shaping the first fully-elected board overseeing the nation's fourth-largest school district.

summaries.headline: Anthropic Joins Crowded Field of Classroom AI Tools
summaries.summary: Anthropic launched Claude for Teachers this week, offering the AI assistant free to verified K-12 educators and positioning it to compete with Google, OpenAI, and Khan Academy for classroom market share. The tool incorporates academic standards from all 50 states and can generate individualized lesson plans by pulling in a student's past assessment data, assignment history, and prior lesson plans; Detroit Public Schools will pilot the product as part of a study on educator well-being. The launch lands amid a widening split in K-12 AI sentiment — with the AFT, the Trump administration, and Bill Gates pushing adoption even as a parent-led backlash against ed-tech contracts and screen time gains traction in some of the country's largest districts.

summaries.headline: Educators Report Rising Fragility in Student Friendships
summaries.summary: Youth mental health continues to deteriorate even as schools add counselors and expand support resources, and the authors argue current interventions still fall short of what students need. A survey of educators across 311 U.S. school districts found that 52% observed student friendships becoming more fragile and conflict-prone compared to two or three years ago, with nearly two-thirds reporting related concerns in their classrooms. The findings point to a gap between clinical mental health supports and the everyday social skills — handling conflict, repairing relationships, reaching out to isolated peers — that schools may need to teach more directly.

summaries.headline: States Must Step Up as Federal Role Shrinks
summaries.summary: State education agencies are being pushed into a leadership role they've rarely held, as federal influence recedes and districts look to states for guidance amid unfinished pandemic learning recovery, falling enrollment, and the expiration of federal relief funds. Districts face compounding pressure from shifting federal funding requirements and rapidly changing civil rights guidance, with one superintendent describing the resulting uncertainty as creating "chaos that ultimately impacts students and families." The authors argue SEAs don't need sweeping reforms to help — often the most effective support comes from small, targeted changes that reduce compliance burden rather than add to it, a distinction that could determine whether states become genuine partners or just another layer of confusion for stretched-thin districts.

summaries.headline: Dover Schools Join Push for Funding Overhaul
summaries.summary: Dover's school board voted 4-to-1 to join the Ohio Coalition for Equity and Adequacy of School Funding, a group now representing more than 250 districts, vocational schools and educational service centers statewide. Superintendent Karie McCrate says the district's decision reflects agreement with the coalition's push for a fairer state funding formula. As more districts sign on, the coalition's growing numbers add pressure on state lawmakers to revisit how Ohio finances its public schools.

summaries.headline: NYC Extends Top Special Ed Programs to Preschool
summaries.summary: New York City is expanding five of its most in-demand special education programs—Nest, Horizon, AIMS, Path, and ACES—into preschool classrooms for the first time, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced this week. The $67.5 million investment adds 250 preschool seats across 26 schools in 14 districts, targeting a long-standing gap where the city has failed to guarantee legally required placements for preschoolers with disabilities even as it built out universal pre-K for typically developing peers. City officials did not say whether the expansion will finally close that gap entirely, leaving open the question of how many families will still face delays before the start of the school year.

summaries.headline: NYC's Para Shortage Strands Students With Disabilities
summaries.summary: A citywide shortage of roughly 1,600 paraprofessionals in New York City is leaving some students with disabilities unable to get to school at all, since bus companies won't transport students without the one-to-one aide their IEP requires. One Bronx student with autism missed more than half of the 2024-25 school year and about a quarter of this past year because his bus repeatedly passed his house without a para on board, while his mother, who works from home, had no way to fill the gap. The union is pushing a $10,000 raise for paras—whose DOE salaries currently range from $34,000 to $57,000—arguing pay is the root cause, but Mayor Mamdani has resisted mandating the increase outside collective bargaining, leaving the staffing crisis and its effect on IEP compliance unresolved as families absorb the consequences.

summaries.headline: CTU Endorses 15 of 21 Chicago Board Seats
summaries.summary: The Chicago Teachers Union announced endorsements in just 15 of 21 school board races up for election in November, a gap that could jeopardize the union's current majority on the board. The slate backs 10 incumbents who previously won CTU support or were appointed by Mayor Brandon Johnson, a former union organizer, while notably excluding Yesenia Lopez, a 2024 CTU-backed winner who has since broken from the bloc on some votes; the union left six races unendorsed where only one candidate is running or no CTU-aligned contender exists. With the union also backing its own political director for board president, the endorsement pattern signals how much is riding on this fall's fully-elected board taking shape amid CTU's push for more state funding.

summaries.headline: Indiana Districts Turn to Voters as State Aid Shrinks
summaries.summary: At least 38 Indiana school districts are asking voters to approve property tax increases this November, a record for a single election cycle, as state policy changes reshape district finances. Lawmakers last year restricted referendum votes to general elections in even-numbered years and passed a property tax relief bill projected to strip districts of millions in revenue, pushing half of the 38 districts to seek early renewals of operating referendums that haven't yet expired and five others to request one for the first time. With the next ballot opportunity two years away, districts are front-loading requests now rather than risk a funding gap later.

summaries.headline: Adult SEL Needs Leadership Priority, Not Lip Service
summaries.summary: District leaders often treat adult social-emotional learning as a feel-good extra—something closer to casual Fridays than a strategic priority—rather than a core leadership function. The framing matters because staff wellbeing and emotional capacity directly shape classroom climate, retention, and how effectively adults model the very SEL competencies students are expected to learn. Districts that continue to sideline adult SEL as optional culture-building risk undermining the broader wellness and instructional goals they claim to prioritize.

summaries.headline: IIT Madras Sets New Bar for Campus Wellness
summaries.summary: IIT Madras has become the first centrally funded technical institution in India to earn ISO certification for its student wellness centre, with the credential awarded by TUV Nord Group for its occupational health and safety management systems. The certification recognizes a structured approach to student wellbeing that includes formal risk identification, preventive interventions, and continuous improvement processes, and the institute paired the announcement with a national workshop on student mental health. As more institutions face pressure to move beyond ad hoc counseling services, IIT Madras's model offers a template for treating wellness infrastructure with the same rigor as academic or safety systems.

Governor Gavin Newsom has signed California’s 2026-27 state budget, which includes several major investments in public education, including increased per-pupil funding, support programs for students with additional needs, and funding aimed at strengthening the educator workforce.

California State Superintendent of Public Instruction Tony Thurmond discussed the budget during remarks at the California State Board of Education meeting, highlighting provisions that align with priorities identified by the California Department of Education.

The budget includes a 4.31% cost-of-living adjustment, described by state officials as a “super COLA,” along with a $5 billion one-time Student Support and Professional Development Discretionary Block Grant. It also provides ongoing funding to expand the Community Schools program.

The spending plan includes $146 million for services supporting students experiencing homelessness, funding tied to Assembly Bill 673, legislation sponsored by Thurmond focused on homeless youth services.

Additional education workforce investments include $428 million for teacher pipeline programs and funding for paid pregnancy leave for educators.

In a statement, Thurmond said the budget includes investments intended to support students, teachers, and school staff. He also raised concerns about the decision to withhold $3.9 billion in Proposition 98 funding, saying schools need stable and predictable funding to maintain programs and services.

The 2026-27 budget continues state investments in programs including universal meals, community schools, and other student support services.

# Northampton Admin updates Board on school funding, housing, infrastructure and future budget planning

July 16, 2026

\|

[Daily News Headlines](https://shoredailynews.com/category/headlines/)

![Northampton County Virginia](https://shoredailynews.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/Northampton-County-Virginia.jpg)

Northampton County Administrator Matt Spuck provided the Board of Supervisors with a wide-ranging update Tuesday, covering topics that included school construction funding, affordable housing, fire and EMS equipment needs, transportation improvements, and early planning for the county’s next budget.

Spuck said the Accomack-Northampton Planning District Commission (A-NPDC) has requested legislative priorities for Fiscal Year 2027. He recommended the Board place the matter on its Aug. 12 agenda to allow sufficient time to submit Northampton County’s priorities for consideration.

### School Construction Funding Strategy

Spuck said county staff continues to work closely with Northampton County Public Schools on the financial strategy for the school construction project.

He told supervisors there is a possibility the project will require additional funding, although the exact amount has not yet been determined.

[![](https://shoredailynews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/ES-Rural-Health-Walkins-Welcome.jpg)](https://esrh.org/walkin-sick-care/)

“We’re going to prepare a unified presentation for you and for the School Board so that we’re both coming at it with exactly the same numbers,” Spuck said, adding that both boards will receive the same financial information before any decisions are made.

### Housing Outreach Tailored to Individual Towns

Spuck also updated the Board on meetings he recently held with town managers and mayors following the Board’s direction to improve communication regarding housing issues.

Rather than using a one-size-fits-all approach, he said each municipality is developing a communication strategy that best fits its residents.

Eastville has indicated that a single, well-publicized town hall meeting would be sufficient, while Cape Charles may use a model similar to the public outreach process it used during discussions about its beach project.

[![](https://shoredailynews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/ANEC-Yellow-and-Black.png)](https://www.anec.com/)

Meanwhile, Cheriton officials expressed concern about low public participation and are considering how to better engage residents.

Spuck said the discussions are focused solely on identifying housing needs and improving public engagement—not on specific housing developments or zoning amendments.

### Opportunity Zones Could Bring Housing Incentives

Spuck introduced supervisors to changes involving federally designated Opportunity Zones.

Northampton County currently has two Opportunity Zones, generally covering the area from Cheriton northward in two census tracts. In the past, the designation was automatic and primarily served as a label for potential investment incentives.

[![Coldwell Banker Harbour Realty](https://shoredailynews.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/Coldwell-Banker-Harbour-Realty-e1681156873791.png)](http://cbharbour.com/)

However, under new federal rules, governors must nominate only 25 percent of eligible census tracts for Opportunity Zone status. Virginia has 607 eligible census tracts, but only about 152 can be nominated.

If Northampton seeks nomination, the designation could make projects eligible for Opportunity Fund investments and Low-Income Housing Tax Credits.

Spuck said the Board will need to decide next month whether it wants the county to pursue the designation before nominations are due to the governor by late September.

Supervisors asked for additional information about how the program would work before making a decision.

[![](https://shoredailynews.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/franktown-jam-SDN-revised.jpg)](https://www.facebook.com/franktownjam/)

### Cape Charles Sewer Study Underway

Spuck said he recently met with representatives of Virginia American Water, the Town of Cape Charles, Atlantic Group and Royal Farms to discuss the possibility of extending sewer service to the Route 13 corridor.

A private entity will fund the engineering study, meaning there will be no cost to county taxpayers.

Royal Farms has expressed interest in locating along the corridor, and one option under consideration is connecting to the county’s Bayview wastewater treatment plant instead of constructing a multimillion-dollar sewer line.

County officials have already met with the Virginia Department of Health to determine whether the concept is feasible.

### Fire Departments Face $20 Million in Apparatus Needs

Following meetings with local volunteer fire departments, Spuck said the county has identified approximately $20 million in fire apparatus replacement needs over the next decade.

Although the county is not legally obligated to purchase equipment for volunteer departments, Spuck said the rising cost of apparatus makes the issue difficult for local departments to address on their own.

He noted that replacing a ladder truck now costs about $3 million, while Cape Charles Volunteer Fire Company is preparing to purchase a new rescue truck at an estimated cost of $900,000.

The recent Cape Charles fire highlighted the importance of ensuring departments have reliable equipment, he said, adding that the county needs to begin discussing how it might help support future apparatus purchases.

### Parallel Road Improvements Being Studied

The county has completed a survey of Parallel Road, providing officials with detailed information on property ownership and right-of-way boundaries.

Spuck said county staff will now work with VDOT and consultants to determine what improvements can be made to improve safety while discouraging motorists from parking along U.S. Route 13.

He noted that a previous engineering estimate put the cost of upgrading Parallel Road to full secondary road standards at approximately $5 million, but officials hope less expensive alternatives may be available.

### Tire Amnesty Program Proposed

Spuck also asked for feedback on pursuing a state grant to establish a temporary tire amnesty program.

The proposal would allow residents and farmers to dispose of old tires at no charge during a limited period.

The Virginia Department of Environmental Quality offers competitive grant funding for such programs, and supervisors voiced support for pursuing the grant application.

### “Northampton Nook” Housing Project Continues

Planning also continues for the proposed “Northampton Nook” workforce housing project intended for educators.

Spuck said engineers are evaluating whether the site can provide an adequate drinking water supply and determining the best wastewater solution.

The preferred option would connect the project to the new wastewater system being constructed near the county administration building, although available capacity remains under review.

Spuck said staff is also evaluating alternative locations should utility challenges prevent development at the current site.

### Early Look at Next Year’s Budget

Finally, Spuck told supervisors county staff has already begun preparing preliminary projections for the Fiscal Year 2028 budget.

Because state salary increases have already been established through the governor’s biennial budget and no countywide reassessment is scheduled next year, he said officials can begin forecasting the budget well in advance.

Spuck said providing supervisors with an early overview will allow more time to review, discuss and adjust spending priorities before the formal budget process begins early next year.

An upcoming joint work session between the Fairbanks North Star Borough Assembly and the Board of Education aims to address one thing: a 2018 ordinance that effectively limits how much the school district can keep in savings.

The Assembly adopted an ordinance in 2018 that restricts the Fairbanks North Star Borough School District’s unrestricted fund balance to 40% of the prior year’s local contribution from the borough.

If audits revealed that the district’s fund balance exceeded the 40% threshold, the surplus would be swept into the school facilities maintenance reserve fund.

The ordinance was adopted in late 2018 amid concerns that the school district had a massive surplus in its fund balance.

“We wanted to give them the opportunity to talk about that ordinance and how the timing of funding works,” said Scott Crass, the Assembly presiding officer. “There’s also a fiduciary responsibility we have as an Assembly as a funding body for the school district. Explaining both those perspectives could be helpful.”

However, the school board argues the ordinance is a severe hindrance to school district operations.

“I don’t think it’s an appropriate ordinance,” said Bobby Burgess, the school board president. “It causes harm to the district by preventing us from saving for future expenses.”

The work session also plans to outline the school district budget process and fund balance, the impact of unanticipated funding and potential solutions.

“From the school board’s perspective, we would like to change it or get rid of it altogether,” Burgess said. “It puts an additional cap on our savings that no other municipality in Alaska has to deal with.”

He said there’s room for discussion and compromise, “but the ordinance in its existing form has to go.”

“We’re looking for stability and to save to plan for the future to achieve that stability,” Burgess said.

Crass said he doesn’t think a straight repeal is something the Assembly will consider. However, he added, “it’s fair for the school board to ask.”

“I do think there might be some ways where we are able to look at funding that lapses from year to year in a way that works for the district,” Crass said. “Our job is to budget a specific amount and make it available for them to use. We don’t want to penalize them if they have more money one year or the next because they may need a shock absorber.”

Crass said the borough has had ordinances on the books since the 1980s that monitor the school district’s fund balance. He said the work session might evaluate whether the concerns from 2018 are still relevant or whether there are other solutions that would allow the borough “to have good fiscal oversight.”

“I want to be educated before I make up my mind on which we should go,” Crass said.

Burgess noted that previous borough ordinances placed guardrails on school district funding but “were much simpler.”

A 2009 ordinance created the school facilities reserve fund, requiring the district to roll over funding into the account. However, several years went by without that happening.

The 2018 ordinance turned everything on its side by classifying all the district’s unrestricted fund accounts, including its self-insurance, risk and transportation funds. The district also received its federal impact aid funding late.

That provision sparked tension between the Assembly and the school board after an audit found an $11.4 million surplus earlier this year. The school district advocated for keeping the entire amount, citing fiscal uncertainty, such as ongoing labor negotiations with its classified and teacher unions.

Burgess said the surplus was unexpected for several reasons, including lower health and workers’ compensation insurance claims and lower enrollment in the district’s health plan.

“That shouldn’t be counted as part of our savings because it’s highly variable and unpredictable,” Burgess said.

Ultimately, the surplus was swept into the maintenance reserve fund, and the Assembly used $5.7 million of that pot for an overall $65.7 million local contribution.

Burgess said the puzzling element is that encumbrances, or funds obligated for items such as purchase orders but not yet spent, are included in the total.

“That’s money that’s already spent, but the borough still counts it as our savings,” Burgess said.

Burgess said he’s concerned about the next fiscal year if the 2018 ordinance remains in place. The Alaska Legislature approved an additional $140 million in one-time funding for education, which Gov. Mike Dunleavy left largely intact. About $115 million is contingent on unexpected revenue the state anticipates from high oil prices between March and June.

The Dunleavy administration hasn’t given guidance on how much districts should anticipate, but Burgess said FNSBSD could receive about $13 million. That amount wasn’t included in the district’s final budget because the one-time funding was approved after the school board adopted its budget.

“We won’t be able to spend most of that, and there’s not a lot of adjustments we can make,” Burgess said. “We’re probably going to have that money sitting in our fund balance at the end of next \[fiscal year\]. We probably can’t spend enough of it to avoid another sweep if this ordinance is in place.”

He said maintenance isn’t the best use of that funding. Instead, it could help with things such as salary increases for teachers and staff.

Crass, the Assembly presiding officer, called the district’s budgeting timeline insane. The district starts its budget cycle before the Alaska Legislature determines the upcoming fiscal year budget and must essentially guess how much it will receive. State law and borough code govern when a district must submit its recommended budget to the Assembly, which determines the final local contribution. The district must then revise and adopt a final budget after the Alaska Legislature approves the state budget.

“It’s just nuts,” Crass said. “It creates this unnecessary chaos every year, reduces flexibility and locks us into budget cycles.”

The joint work session will take place at 5:30 p.m. Thursday at the Juanita Helms Administration Center, 907 Terminal St.

# South Bristol Education Budget Up 11.09%

January 26, 2023

![South Bristol Education Budget Up 11.09%](https://lcnme.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/06/Current-News.jpg)

The South Bristol School Committee and the town’s budget committee approved the 2023-2024 fiscal year education budget during a joint meeting at the school on Tuesday, Jan. 17.

The budget totals $2,530,872.97, up $252,856.92, or 11.09%.

Because of a carry-forward of funds from last year’s budget of $165,000 and the final year of a private annual donation of $75,000, the tax impact on South Bristol residents will total $2,153,085.16, up $121,490.93 or 6%.

The impact depends on what the state subsidy is for the school as well, which is not yet known, but is estimated from last year’s amount of $138,787.81.

# Jefferson Education Budget Faces Validation Vote For Third Time

[Christina Brown](https://lcnme.com/staff_name/christina-brown/)

October 31, 2025

![Jefferson Education Budget Faces Validation Vote For Third Time](https://lcnme.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/06/Current-News.jpg)

Residents of Jefferson will consider whether to validate the proposed education budget during the referendum election on Tuesday, Nov. 4, the town’s third attempt at passing an education budget for the 2026 fiscal year.

The education budget as proposed totals $9,369,346.88, an increase from last year’s budget of $818,950.30 or 9.58%.

The proposal is a decrease, however, of $677,470.98 or 6.97% from the second version of the budget, which voters approved at a special town meeting on July 9 but failed to validate at the polls on Aug. 12 with a vote of 279-152.

The Jefferson School Committee originally put forward a $9,763,805.37 education budget in May, which residents approved at a special town meeting May 21 but failed to validate at the polls June 10 with a vote of 92-90.

The figure voters will face at the polls, which is the lowest of the three drafts presented this year, was approved by the Jefferson school and budget committees on Sept. 9. Residents voted to approve the budget at a special town meeting on Oct. 1 at Jefferson Village School.

AOS 93 Superintendent Todd Sanders said at the Oct. 1 special town meeting that the main driver in budget increases has been the special education budget and the town’s need to pay out-of-district tuition costs for special education services due to a lack of staff at JVS.

“We had a significant shortage of teachers and support staff in special education for the 2024-2025 school year,” Sanders said. “That necessitated us paying out-of-district tuition for students, special purpose tuitions, and hiring contracted service providers, which cost much more than a certified teacher that we’ve hired ourselves.”

Sanders said that due to an increase in staff, more students were able to be educated at JVS, The budget for special education is $2,686,882.74, a decrease of $545,986.98 or 16.88% from the version the school committee approved in July.

Compared to what voters approved in fiscal year 2025, the budget categories are as follows: regular instruction totals $3,437,892.65, an increase of $101,247.49 or 3.03%; special instruction totals $2,686,882.74, an increase of $688,149.11 or 34.43%; career and technical education is $100, the same as last year; other instruction is $43,202, a decrease of $4,900 or 10.19%; student and staff support is $435,752.08, a decrease of $32,837.46 or 7.01%; system administration is $284,804.43, an increase of $47,990.40 or 19.81%; school administration is $292,515.10, a decrease of $68,757.86 or 19.03%; transportation is $677,500.47, an increase of $153,975.49 or 29.41%; facilities and maintenance totals $664,747.97, a decrease of $55,461.43 or 7.7%; debt services is $783,949.44, a decrease of $19,564.44 or 2.43%; and food service totals $60,000, an increase of $10,000 or 20%.

The polls will be open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. at the Jefferson fire department, at 204 Waldoboro Road in Jefferson. For more information, go to [aos93.org/o/jvs](http://aos93.org/o/jvs) or call 506-3044.

# Pothole Fixes, New Doors Included in Edgecomb’s $4.5 Million Education Budget

[Emily Bracher](https://lcnme.com/staff_name/emily-bracher/)

May 3, 2026

![Pothole Fixes, New Doors Included in Edgecomb’s $4.5 Million Education Budget](https://lcnme.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/06/Current-News.jpg)

Edgecomb residents will consider a $4,539,384 education budget at a special town meeting at 10 a.m. on Saturday, May 2.

The recommended budget is a $380,731 or 9.2% increase from last year. Taxpayers will be responsible for a total of $3,503,673, a $520,250 or 17.4% increase.

The Edgecomb School Committee initially recommended the budget in early March after two three-hour meetings. Committee Chair Heather Sinclair voiced her frustration at the March meetings, saying the process of funding education can be difficult and uncontrollable.

The sharp increase to the taxpayers’ responsibility, according to Heather Sinclair, is due in part to the school committee not knowing how much of the unassigned fund balance could be used to offset taxes. She anticipates an amendment will come be considered at the May 2 meeting regarding the utilization of those funds to lower the tax assessment.

“Education is expensive, but education in Edgecomb is not abnormally expensive,” Sinclair said. “The cost per student as calculated by the state is slightly above state average but below several surrounding districts.”

The budget includes an anticipated increase in special education needs, a proposed lease agreement with First Student for a bus, and funding to hire a full-time kitchen faculty member.

The $927,221 special education budget is up $79,830 or 9.4%. Sinclair said the rise is to ensure Edgecomb has adequate services for special education students.

The facilities and maintenance budget totals $371,480, an increase of $29,704 or 8.7%. Within this budget is the elementary school repair and maintenance budget, which totals $47,000, an increase of $26,000 or 123.8%. A portion of the funds is for a project to replace the exterior doors of Edgecomb Eddy School.

The school committee will use a separate warrant article outside of the budget to look at raising funds to address the pothole in the Edgecomb Eddy School driveway.

The transportation and buses budget totals $187,317, a decrease of $3,350 or 1.8%.

Edgecomb’s two school buses are five years into what usually is a 10-year lifecycle for New England school buses, Sinclair said. To avoid having to purchase a brand new bus two years in a row, the school committee agreed to ask the administration to look into leasing one bus from First Student. The potential lease cost of $35,000 is included in the budget.

Elsewhere, $68,808 has been put aside for other expenditures, which is an increase of $33,808 or 96.6%. The rise is in anticipation of the hiring of a full-time kitchen staff Selectionmember at Edgecomb Eddy.

“The proposed change covers the cost of switching from a contracted service to in house kitchen staff,” Sinclair said. “The costs of food and food preparation are covered by state and federal grants that Edgecomb currently sends to the community school district.”

The regular instruction budget totals $2,456,311, an increase of $221,664 or 9.9%. Sinclair said the increase covers contractual salary increases, uncontrollable health insurance increases, and changes in secondary education tuition costs.

The other instruction budget totals $4,000, an increase of $549 or 15.9%. Within this budget is the outdoor experience of Edgecomb Eddy’s sixth grade students, Sinclair said.

“We have moved away from Chewonki, a longstanding tradition, and towards Hearty Roots in an effort to cut costs and continue to develop a relationship with this amazing organization,” Sinclair said.

System administration totals $183,402, an increase of $27,585 or 17.7%. Sinclair said the system administration budget covers Edgecomb’s portion of AOS 98 costs. This year is the second year of bringing a director of technology to the school district’s budget, which accounts for the increase.

“We anticipate this flattening out next year,” Sinclair said.

In other areas of the education budget, the student and staff support budget totals $118,959, a decrease of $3,218 or 2.6%, and the school administration budget totals $221,886, a decrease of $5,841 or 2.6%.

Not everyone in town is happy with this year’s recommended budget, Sinclair said. Throughout the budget process, she and the select board have faced pressure from many residents who are upset about the rising taxes. Unfortunately, Sinclair said, a lot of the rising costs are out of the school committee’s hands.

Like many other towns across the county, Sinclair said Edgecomb doesn’t receive as much state subsidy because of property valuations. Because of the state subsidy formula, the assessment passed on to the taxpayer is high, she said.

“Very little of the budget is directly controllable during the annual budget process,” Sinclair said. “The larger work around developing long-term plans and advocating for changes in revenue is a top priority for the board all year. We are proud of the work we have done to support tuition in students to add to our classrooms and bring in revenue, and over our advocacy work.”

There will be an open town meeting at 10 a.m. on Saturday, May 2 at Edgecomb Eddy School for the consideration of the education budget.

Voters will then consider validating the budget at the polls on Saturday, May 16, which coincides with the annual town meeting by referendum and election of municipal officers. Polls will be open from 1-7 p.m.

For more information, call 882-7018 or go to [edgecomb.org](http://edgecomb.org/).

# Jefferson Voters to Weigh Validation of $9.8 Million Education Budget

[Molly Rains](https://lcnme.com/staff_name/molly-rains/)

June 5, 2025

![Jefferson Voters to Weigh Validation of $9.8 Million Education Budget](https://lcnme.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/06/Current-News.jpg)

Jefferson voters will consider whether to accept a $9.8 million education budget at the polls on Tuesday, June 10.

The budget marks an increase of $1,184,104.88 or 13.85% over last year. About 50 voters approved the budget with little discussion during a special town meeting on Wednesday, May 21.

Much of the increase is due to Jefferson Village School being shortstaffed, particularly in the school’s special education department, said Jefferson School Committee Chair Danielle Bernier. The school must send students to other programs that they do not have the staff to provide themselves, or pay for contracted services, she said; schools are legally required to provide these special educational services.

# RSU 12 Recommends $30 Million Education Budget

[Emily Bracher](https://lcnme.com/staff_name/emily-bracher/)

April 16, 2026

![RSU 12 Recommends $30 Million Education Budget](https://lcnme.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/06/Current-News.jpg)

The RSU 12 Board of Directors unanimously recommended a $30,038,306.13 education budget for the upcoming fiscal year at its meeting on Thursday, April 10.

The vote follows budget presentations to the towns of RSU 12 – Alna, Chelsea, Palermo, Somerville, Whitefield, Windsor, and Westport Island – by Superintendent Howard Tuttle over the past few weeks.

“I feel like we did the best we could,” Tuttle said.

The recommended budget is a $1,397,579.31 or 4.8% increase from last fiscal year. The total estimated local cost is $16,810,192.96, an increase of 698,676.78 or 4.2%.

The local cost-sharing formula leaves Whitefield responsible for $3,260,332.51, an increase of $165,687.73 or 5.8%; Alna responsible for $1,284,870.39, an increase of $69,385.88 or 5.2%; Somerville responsible for $774,786.05, an increase of $5,363 or 0.6%; and Westport Island responsible for $1,118,094.76, an increase of $61,692.31 or 5.8%.

Chelsea’s contribution will be for $3,315,890.64, an increase of $84,342.02 or 2.6%; Palermo’s totals $2,557,573.96, an increase of $104,051.06 or 4.2%; and Windsor will contribute for $4,398,644.65, an increase of $298,156.34 or 4.9%.

Over 70% of the budget is allocated for regular instruction, secondary tuition, and special education. The recommended regular instruction budget totals $6,508,229, an increase of $128,883.51 or 2%. Tuition for secondary education is budgeted at $8,734,625.75, an increase of $612,523.55 or 7.5%. Special education is budgeted at $6,311,880.43, an increase of $190,458.75 or 3.11%.

The $2,344,295.53 facilities and maintenance budget is an increase of $192,381.87 or 8.94%. Tuttle said the budgeted amount is for roof repairs at Whitefield Elementary School.

Other areas of the budget include other instruction at $179,660, an increase of $22,001.95 or 13.96%; student and staff support at $1,353,698.69, an increase of $45,115.53 or 3.44%; system administration at $825,968.77, an increase of $64,024.89 or 8.40%; school administration at $1,063,460.39, an increase of $72,887.66 or 7.36%; transportation and buses at $1,862,385.22, an increase of $59,301.60 or 3.29%; and debt service at $854,102.35, an increase of $10,000 or 1.18%.

Future of costs of education may possibly go down if the town of Liberty decides to join RSU 12, Tuttle said.

Liberty is currently exploring withdrawal from RSU 3; the town’s students then would attend Palermo School. The estimated financial impact if Liberty would join RSU 12 is all current towns in school district would see approximately a 5% decrease in their local contribution, Tuttle said.

Tuttle said there have not been any final decisions about the discussed addition and he plans on meeting with officials from Liberty at the end of the month.

At the board’s March meeting, Tuttle said costs district officials have control over, such as staffing, salaries, and benefits, have increased by $128,883.51 or 2%.

According to Tuttle, the district’s uncontrollable costs include regular tuition, special education tuition, and the $222,842 increase in insured value factor, which is used to pay for building upkeep and critical maintenance at private schools. In 2025, the Maine Department of Education raised the insured value factor from being 6% of the maximum allowable tuition to 10%.

For the upcoming fiscal year, Tuttle said RSU 12 expects to receive $13,228,113.17 in state subsidy and other revenue, an increase of $698,902.53 or 5.58%.

Since the beginning of budget season, Tuttle has been a fierce advocate for L.D. 2226, “An Act to Amend the Essential Programs and Services School Funding Formula,” because he believes if passed, the bill will help the towns in RSU 12 that receive the least state subsidy.

State subsidy given to schools is currently dependent on the Essential Programs and Services funding formula that takes into account property taxes across the state, using home sales to determine property values. The higher the property tax, the less amount of funding the school receives from the state, Tuttle said.

In Tuttle’s presentation, he said RSU 12 property valuations have increased $248,166,667 or 15.05% in the last year, the state’s subsidy formula penalizing those with fast-rising property values by minimizing or eliminating state aid.

If passed, L.D. 2226 would make changes to the model that determines state subsidy, which has been in place since 2005. L.D. 2226 would still consider property tax, but would also take into consideration factors such as the community household income. If the bill is passed as proposed, previously disadvantaged districts would receive more support from the state, Tuttle said.

“Hopefully L.D. 2226 will pass and hopefully Liberty will join us,” Tuttle said.

Residents from the towns that make up RSU 12 will consider the budget during a meeting at 6:30 p.m. on Wednesday, May 20 at Chelsea Elementary School. The validation vote will be held on Tuesday, June 9 at each town’s polling locations.

![Edgecomb Eddy School Officials Talk Community Outreach, School Funding](https://lcnme.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/06/Current-News.jpg)

Edgecomb Eddy School was abuzz with community members the night of Tuesday, Oct. 28.

In an effort to give Edgecomb residents a look into the school’s operations and goals, school staff and committee officials discussed plans for community outreach and the school’s financial status during the address.

The Edgecomb Select Board moved its regular meeting to the elementary school to encourage public participation and attendance for the address, board Chair Michael Maxim said.

Principal Laura Mewa shared several plans like organizing community workout classes or turning the school library into a public library for the town of Edgecomb and kids to utilize.

# Tri County school funding renewal proposal won’t raise taxes on primary homes

[Open Audio Article Player](https://www.thedailynews.cc/audio-articles/player/audio-article-381181)

[By Elisabeth Waldon](https://www.thedailynews.cc/author/ewaldon/)

on
July 13, 2026

Voters within the Tri County Area Schools district will be asked in the Aug. 4 primary election to consider renewing the district’s non-homestead operating millage. The ballot proposal seeks to replace the expiring millage and allow the district to continue to levy the statutory rate of not to exceed 18 mills ($18 per each $1,000 of taxable value) on non-homestead property only.
